Reference: Farrokhi and Lashkaripour (2025)

Model Setting

The paper asks how far trade policy can go in solving the free-riding problem in international climate agreements. Each government cares only about the climate damage borne by its own residents, so the unilaterally optimal carbon tax is far below the social cost of carbon. Two trade-policy remedies are evaluated: (1) noncooperative carbon border taxes, which tax the carbon content of foreign goods directly; and (2) Nordhaus's (2015) climate club, in which members raise carbon taxes to a common target and threaten nonmembers with trade penalties. The paper builds a multi-country, multi-industry general equilibrium trade model with a global carbon supply chain, derives closed-form formulas for unilaterally optimal carbon and border taxes using a dual decomposition technique, and uses these formulas to compute the policy frontier of both proposals with GTAP 2014 data (19 countries/regions, 17 nonenergy industries plus energy).

Production is a two-stage process: (1) each country's energy industry (k=0k=0k=0) uses labor and carbon reserves to extract energy, which is traded internationally; (2) final-good industries (k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,Kk=1,…,K) combine labor and an energy bundle to produce goods, which are also traded. CO2_22​ is counted when energy is used by final-good producers and households. Markets are perfectly competitive, and no private agent internalizes the effect of its choices on global emissions.

Welfare and the Unilateral Policy Problem

The welfare of country iii is consumption utility net of the disutility from global emissions:

Wi=Vi(Ei,P~i)−δi×Z(global)(9.2.1.11)W_i=V_i(E_i,\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_i)-\delta_i\times Z^{(global)} \tag{9.2.1.11}Wi​=Vi​(Ei​,P~i​)−δi​×Z(global)(9.2.1.11)

where δi\delta_iδi​ is the disutility per ton of CO2_22​ as perceived by country iii's government. Let Ii≡{tji,k,xij,k,τi,k}j,k\mathbb{I}_i\equiv\{t_{ji,k},x_{ij,k},\tau_{i,k}\}_{j,k}Ii​≡{tji,k​,xij,k​,τi,k​}j,k​ be country iii's instruments. The unilaterally optimal policy maximizes national welfare taking foreign policies Iˉ−i\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{-i}Iˉ−i​ as given:

Ii∗=arg⁡max⁡IiWi(Ii;Iˉ−i)subject to general equilibrium conditions(9.2.1.12)\mathbb{I}_i^*=\arg\max_{\mathbb{I}_i}W_i(\mathbb{I}_i;\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{-i})\quad\text{subject to general equilibrium conditions} \tag{9.2.1.12}Ii∗​=argIi​max​Wi​(Ii​;Iˉ−i​)subject to general equilibrium conditions(9.2.1.12)

It corrects two inefficiencies from iii's standpoint: (1) the climate externality of domestic and foreign emissions on iii's residents, and (2) iii's unexploited collective market power (terms of trade). By the targeting principle, domestic carbon taxes address domestic emissions, carbon border taxes address foreign emissions, and uniform border taxes manipulate the terms of trade.

Dual Decomposition

Instead of choosing taxes, the government directly chooses after-tax prices Pi={P~ji,k,P~ij,k,τi,k}j,k\mathbb{P}_i=\{\tilde{P}_{ji,k},\tilde{P}_{ij,k},\tau_{i,k}\}_{j,k}Pi​={P~ji,k​,P~ij,k​,τi,k​}j,k​, and taxes are recovered as 1+tji,k∗=P~ji,k∗/Pji,k1+t_{ji,k}^*=\tilde{P}_{ji,k}^*/P_{ji,k}1+tji,k∗​=P~ji,k∗​/Pji,k​ and (1+xij,k∗)−1=P~ij,k∗/Pij,k(1+x_{ij,k}^*)^{-1}=\tilde{P}_{ij,k}^*/P_{ij,k}(1+xij,k∗​)−1=P~ij,k∗​/Pij,k​. Global Optimum and Free-Riding

A global planner chooses all instruments and lump-sum transfers to maximize ∑iϑiln⁡Wi\sum_i\vartheta_i\ln W_i∑i​ϑi​lnWi​. The globally optimal policy taxes carbon at the sum of all countries' disutilities and sets all border taxes to zero, since carbon taxes target emissions directly:

τi,k⋆=∑iδ~i≡τ⋆,tij,k⋆=xij,k⋆=0(∀i,j,k)(9.2.1.18)\tau_{i,k}^\star=\sum_i\tilde{\delta}_i\equiv\tau^\star,\qquad t_{ij,k}^\star=x_{ij,k}^\star=0\quad(\forall i,j,k) \tag{9.2.1.18}τi,k⋆​=i∑​δ~i​≡τ⋆,tij,k⋆​=xij,k⋆​=0(∀i,j,k)(9.2.1.18)

The free-riding problem is the gap τi∗=δ~i<τ⋆=∑nδ~n\tau_i^*=\tilde{\delta}_i<\tau^\star=\sum_n\tilde{\delta}_nτi∗​=δ~i​<τ⋆=∑n​δ~n​: if all others commit to τ⋆\tau^\starτ⋆, each country wants to lower its own tax to δ~i\tilde{\delta}_iδ~i​, triggering a race to the bottom. The paper evaluates two remedies:

  • Proposal 1 (carbon border taxes): every government adopts the unilaterally optimal carbon and border taxes of Proposition 2 noncooperatively. The resulting equilibrium is the Nash equilibrium of a one-shot policy game.

  • Proposal 2 (climate club): a set of core countries N(core)\mathbb{N}^{(core)}N(core) sets a carbon tax target τ(target)\tau^{(target)}τ(target). Members raise domestic carbon taxes to τ(target)\tau^{(target)}τ(target), keep free trade among members, and impose the unilaterally optimal trade taxes (t∗,x∗)(t^*,x^*)(t∗,x∗) of Proposition 2 as penalties on nonmembers. Nonmembers retaliate with their own optimal trade taxes against members but otherwise keep status quo policies.

A partition into members and nonmembers is a Nash equilibrium of the club game if no noncore country wants to switch sides and every core country is better off than in the status quo:

Wi(N(member))≥Wi(N(member)∖{i})  ∀i∈N(member),Wi(N(member))≥Wi(N(member)∪{i})  ∀i∈N(nonmember)(9.2.1.19)W_i\left(\mathbb{N}^{(member)}\right)\ge W_i\left(\mathbb{N}^{(member)}\setminus\{i\}\right)\ \ \forall i\in\mathbb{N}^{(member)},\qquad W_i\left(\mathbb{N}^{(member)}\right)\ge W_i\left(\mathbb{N}^{(member)}\cup\{i\}\right)\ \ \forall i\in\mathbb{N}^{(nonmember)} \tag{9.2.1.19}Wi​(N(member))≥Wi​(N(member)∖{i})  ∀i∈N(member),Wi​(N(member))≥Wi​(N(member)∪{i})  ∀i∈N(nonmember)(9.2.1.19)

A higher target cuts more emissions per member but discourages participation, so emission reductions are inverted-U (Laffer-curve) shaped in τ(target)\tau^{(target)}τ(target). Since penalties are meant to deter rather than be used, the target is set at the maximal rate that still supports a club of all nations.

Quantitative Strategy

The counterfactual equilibrium under optimal policy jointly solves two mappings: (a) the equilibrium given taxes, RV=g(RT;B)\mathcal{R}_V=g(\mathcal{R}_T;\mathcal{B})RV​=g(RT​;B), solved in exact hat algebra relative to the 2014 status quo; and (b) the optimal tax formulas given the equilibrium, RT=f(RV;B)\mathcal{R}_T=f(\mathcal{R}_V;\mathcal{B})RT​=f(RV​;B). The algorithm iterates between the two. Required inputs B\mathcal{B}B are observed baseline shares (expenditure, employment, emissions, energy cost shares, carbon intensities), applied 2014 taxes, and parameters {δ~i,φi,ς,σk}\{\tilde{\delta}_i,\varphi_i,\varsigma,\sigma_k\}{δ~i​,φi​,ς,σk​}. For the club game, the optimal penalties come from the closed-form formulas, avoiding numerical optimization over 2N−N(core)2^{N-N^{(core)}}2N−N(core) partitions. Instead, an iterative procedure (similar to iterated elimination of dominated strategies) adds countries that gain from joining given the current club, until convergence. An outer loop raises τ(target)\tau^{(target)}τ(target) until universal membership fails.

Data and Parameters

  • Trade and emissions: GTAP 2014, aggregated to 19 regions (13 largest economies plus 6 aggregates) and 18 industries; trade imbalances purged as in Ossa (2016). Emissions are counted at the point of energy use. About three-fourths of emissions come from production, and industries with trade-to-GDP below 0.15 (e.g. transportation, over 25% of industrial emissions) account for over 80% of production emissions.

  • Cost shares: αn,k\alpha_{n,k}αn,k​ from sales and energy expenditures; the reserve share φi\varphi_iφi​ from the natural-resource value added share in primary energy (average 0.37).

  • Carbon disutility: δ~i\tilde{\delta}_iδ~i​ is recovered from governments' revealed preferences. Per capita disutility is proportional to environmentally related taxes per ton of CO2_22​ (OECD-PINE), and disutilities add up to the social cost of carbon (EPA, $156.2/tCO2_22​ in 2014):

Key Results

  • Optimal border taxes: absent climate concerns, the median optimal tariff-to-subsidy wedge (1+t∗)/(1+x∗)(1+t^*)/(1+x^*)(1+t∗)/(1+x∗) is 1.17 (10th-90th percentile 1.12-1.26); carbon border components are a modest share and are larger in carbon-intensive industries and for countries with high δ~i\tilde{\delta}_iδ~i​.

  • Proposal 1: unilaterally optimal domestic carbon taxes alone cut global CO2_22​ by 5.4%; adding optimal carbon border taxes cuts it by 6.6%, an extra 1.3%. First-best global carbon taxes cut emissions by 41.0% (an extra 37.6% relative to unilateral carbon taxes). Carbon border taxes thus deliver only 1.3/37.6=3.4%1.3/37.6=3.4\%1.3/37.6=3.4% of the cooperative reduction, while lowering global real consumption by 0.5%. First-best taxes cost 0.6% of real consumption but raise climate-adjusted welfare by 1.1%.

  • Border taxes fail for three reasons: (1) they are based on country-industry average carbon intensity, so individual firms have no incentive to abate; (2) they cannot reach nontraded goods, which account for most emissions; (3) they lower world energy demand and pre-tax energy prices, causing leakage (emissions rise in Russia, Saudi Arabia, Canada).

  • Proposal 2: the maximal carbon tax target supporting universal membership is $36/tCO2_22​ with the EU as core (13.4% emissions cut), $53 with EU+US (18.6%), and $89 with EU+US+China (28.0%), the last one achieving 28.0/41.0≈68%28.0/41.0\approx68\%28.0/41.0≈68% of the first-best reduction. With EU+US as core, the club expands over six rounds following the gravity structure of trade (Brazil, Canada, Korea, Turkey first; Australia and India last), i.e. from West to East.

  • Clubs outperform border taxes because penalties are used as an enforcement device that induces domestic carbon taxes (which reach all firms and nontraded goods), and because members pool their market power into harsher penalties.

Extensions

  • Robustness: results are similar with SC-CO2=92_2=922​=92, country-level social costs of carbon, a common trade elasticity, Cobb-Douglas production (ς→1\varsigma\to1ς→1), or a less elastic energy supply (φi/(1−φi)=2\varphi_i/(1-\varphi_i)=2φi​/(1−φi​)=2). An IV-style test following Adao, Costinot and Donaldson (2025), using 2014-2022 carbon tax changes, does not reject the model.

  • Cooperative border taxes (second-best when first-best carbon taxes are politically infeasible) cut global emissions by only 0.9%. If the EU puts weight on foreign welfare, its policy frontier shows that the “externality-free” policy cuts global emissions by 3.4% but raises leakage. Under unilateral policy the EU can at best cut global emissions by about 5%, compared to over 13% in an EU-led club.

  • Increasing returns to scale (Krugman): optimal policy adds a carbon-blind production subsidy si,k∗=1/(γk−1)s_{i,k}^*=1/(\gamma_k-1)si,k∗​=1/(γk​−1), and carbon border taxes are scaled down by (γk−1)/γk(\gamma_k-1)/\gamma_k(γk​−1)/γk​ because output contraction raises emissions per unit. Relative efficacy of the two proposals is unchanged; the formulas also cover Melitz-Pareto economies.

This is the government's objective. The first term is the indirect utility from consuming final goods, which depends on expenditure EiE_iEi​ and local consumer prices P~i\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_iP~i​. The second term is the climate damage: δi\delta_iδi​ is the utility loss that country iii's government attaches to one ton of CO2_22​, multiplied by global emissions Z(global)Z^{(global)}Z(global) from equation (8). Three assumptions are embedded. (a) Damage is linear in emissions, so the marginal damage is the constant δi\delta_iδi​ regardless of the level of emissions; this is what makes the optimal carbon tax in equation (15) a simple constant. (b) Damage is additively separable from consumption, so emissions do not shift demand. (c) Only the global total matters, not its location, so a ton emitted abroad hurts iii as much as a ton emitted at home.

Since ViV_iVi​ is in utility units, converting the damage into money requires the marginal utility of income:

δ~i≡δi∂Vi/∂Ei=δiP~i,\tilde{\delta}_i\equiv\frac{\delta_i}{\partial V_i/\partial E_i}=\delta_i\tilde{P}_i ,δ~i​≡∂Vi​/∂Ei​δi​​=δi​P~i​,

the amount of income country iii would give up to avoid one ton of emissions. This δ~i\tilde{\delta}_iδ~i​ is the object calibrated in equation (20) and the unilaterally optimal carbon tax. The free-riding problem is visible directly in the objective: the damage that iii's emissions impose on others, ∑n≠iδnZ(global)\sum_{n\ne i}\delta_nZ^{(global)}∑n=i​δn​Z(global), is absent from WiW_iWi​. Each private agent ignores the second term altogether, which is why some policy is needed even from the purely national point of view. The same WiW_iWi​ is used to evaluate membership decisions in equation (19).

This defines the unilaterally optimal policy as a best response. Country iii's government chooses its full set of instruments Ii={tji,k,xij,k,τi,k}j,k\mathbb{I}_i=\{t_{ji,k},x_{ij,k},\tau_{i,k}\}_{j,k}Ii​={tji,k​,xij,k​,τi,k​}j,k​, that is, tariffs on every imported variety, subsidies on every exported variety, and carbon taxes on every end use, to maximize the welfare of equation (11). Foreign policies Iˉ−i\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{-i}Iˉ−i​ are held fixed, so there is no retaliation within this problem. The constraint is that prices, quantities, wages and emissions adjust to the policy according to the full general equilibrium: equations (1) to (10) together with Ei=YiE_i=Y_iEi​=Yi​ and goods market clearing.

Two wedges exist between private and national incentives, and the instruments are assigned to them by the targeting principle. The climate externality on iii's own residents from domestic emissions is corrected by τi,k\tau_{i,k}τi,k​; the externality from foreign emissions, which iii cannot tax directly, is addressed indirectly through carbon-related border taxes; and the country's collective market power in world markets is exploited through the uniform components of border taxes. The policy is optimal only for iii: it ignores the damage on foreigners and deliberately shifts income from them.

The difficulty is that WiW_iWi​ depends on Ii\mathbb{I}_iIi​ through a large system of general equilibrium responses. Equation (13) shows how to solve the problem without computing them, and equations (15) and (16) give the solution. When every country plays Ii∗\mathbb{I}_i^*Ii∗​ simultaneously, the result is the Nash equilibrium of Proposal 1; the same trade taxes serve as the penalties in the climate club of equation (19). The solution is not unique in levels: by Lerner symmetry, a uniform shift of all import taxes and export subsidies leaves the allocation unchanged, hence the shifter tˉi\bar{t}_itˉi​.

This is the Pigou-Samuelson rule: the tax on a ton of CO2_22​ equals the sum of all countries' marginal damages, in every country and industry. Border taxes are zero for two reasons: every ton is already taxed at its source, so there is no untaxed foreign externality left to reach indirectly, and terms-of-trade manipulation is a pure transfer that the planner can make without distortion using Θi\Theta_iΘi​. Comparing with equation (15), each country acting alone internalizes only its own term, τi∗=δ~i<τ⋆\tau_i^*=\tilde{\delta}_i<\tau^\starτi∗​=δ~i​<τ⋆; with the calibration of equation (20), even the EU's δ~i\tilde{\delta}_iδ~i​ is about one third of τ⋆\tau^\starτ⋆.

These inequalities define a Nash equilibrium of the membership stage of the climate club game. Wi(⋅)W_i(\cdot)Wi​(⋅) is country iii's welfare from equation (11), evaluated at the general equilibrium that results when the set in the argument (together with the core N(core)\mathbb{N}^{(core)}N(core)) forms the club: members charge the carbon tax τ(target)\tau^{(target)}τ(target), trade freely with each other, and impose the penalty tariffs and export taxes of equations (15) and (16) on nonmembers, who retaliate with their own optimal trade taxes.

The first inequality is internal stability: no member gains by leaving. Leaving saves the consumption cost of the higher carbon tax but exposes the country to the club's trade penalties (and it gives up the terms-of-trade gains from penalizing others). The second is external stability: no nonmember gains by joining. Core countries do not choose; they are only required to be better off than in the status quo, otherwise they would not launch the club. Each comparison is a unilateral deviation holding other countries' membership fixed, which is what makes this a Nash rather than a coalition-proof concept.

The carbon tax target governs the trade-off. For a low τ(target)\tau^{(target)}τ(target), joining is cheap and universal membership is an equilibrium; as the target rises the cost of membership grows relative to the fixed penalty, some countries prefer to stay out, and the club shrinks. Total abatement is therefore hump-shaped in the target, and the analysis picks the largest target for which the grand club is still an equilibrium. In that equilibrium the penalties are never applied; they work purely as a threat. Checking all 2N−N(core)2^{N-N^{(core)}}2N−N(core) partitions is avoided by iteratively adding countries whose best response is to join, which is feasible only because the penalties are available in closed form.

Each country's money-metric disutility is a share of the global social cost of carbon, with shares proportional to population times the effective environmental tax per ton. The first condition is a revealed-preference assumption: a government that taxes carbon more heavily per ton is taken to care more, per resident, about emissions. Only relative tax rates are used; the level is disciplined by the second condition, which says that a planner adding up all national valuations would arrive at the EPA figure of 156.2 dollars per ton, consistent with τ⋆=∑iδ~i\tau^\star=\sum_i\tilde{\delta}_iτ⋆=∑i​δ~i​ in equation (18). For instance, the EU's value of 53.2 dollars corresponds to a share 53.2/156.2≈0.3453.2/156.2\approx0.3453.2/156.2≈0.34. Note that the proportionality is imposed on per capita disutility; it is a calibration assumption and not an implication of equation (15), under which an optimizing government's tax per ton would equal δ~i\tilde{\delta}_iδ~i​ itself.
